model_comparison.decision_protocol: Deployed model stays RandomForest unless Logistic Regression's best CV macro-F1 clearly exceeds RandomForest's best + 1 std -- not just a nominally higher number. Logistic Regression did not clear that bar, so RandomForest was kept.

headline_generalization_metric.name: 5-fold GroupKFold macro-F1 (group=test_id, all 35 raw sessions)
headline_generalization_metric.note: Report THIS number, not any single-split test accuracy, as this model's expected performance. No held-out test set is used at all for this classifier -- with only 35 raw sessions and as few as 5 groups for the rarest class (Heave), carving out a separate held-out split the way ml/'s vision model does would leave too few groups for either the CV estimate or the held-out set to mean anything. This CV number itself should also be read with real caution given how few groups back up each class.

ceiling_effect_warning: CV macro-F1 hit ~1.0 for BOTH RandomForest and Logistic Regression across every setting tested (RF: every regularization strength incl. the unregularized baseline; LR: every C value tested). This is a red flag, not a win -- treated with the same suspicion this project applied to the vision model's raw-landmark LSTM hitting 100% test accuracy (flagged as shortcut learning, not celebrated). Direct cause, confirmed by inspecting the feature distributions: drift_max alone separates Drag (21.5-32.7) from every other class (max ~12.7 elsewhere) with a huge gap, and flex_range separates Half (53-83) and Heave (101-115) from the rest almost as cleanly -- a 2-threshold decision boundary already gets this perfectly, whether that boundary is found by a shallow tree or a linear model. Both model families agreeing (if both hit the ceiling) is actually further evidence for this diagnosis, not against it: it means the classes are cleanly separable in this feature space by essentially any reasonable classifier, which is exactly what a mechanically-constructed, deliberately-exaggerated, single-person test protocol would produce. This is not evidence either model has learned anything robust or generalizable -- it says nothing about performance on a different person, a genuinely ambiguous rep, or subtler real-world form errors, only that both can tell these 35 staged, exaggerated demonstrations apart.
no_lstm_comparison_note: No LSTM was trained or compared for this dataset. ml/'s vision model already established, with 34 training recordings, that a raw-landmark LSTM shows shortcut-learning symptoms and loses to RandomForest on engineered features. This dataset has fewer independent groups (35 total, several classes with only 5-8 groups), so training an LSTM here would be an even more foregone conclusion than it already was for the vision model -- skipped explicitly, not silently.
